chapter.name: Probability
chapter.blurb: The chapter introduces the conditional probability of an event given that another event has occurred, and uses it to obtain the multiplication rule of probability and the idea of independent events. It then defines a partition of a sample space, proves the theorem of total probability and applies Bayes' theorem to find the reverse probability of a cause once an outcome is known.

scope_in.item: Explain conditional probability P(E|F) as the probability of E when the sample space is reduced to F, and compute it for equally likely outcomes as n(E and F)/n(F) for coins, dice, cards, children and counting situations

Use the definition P(E|F) = P(E and F)/P(F), P(F) not 0, with given probabilities (including finding P(A and B) or P(A or B) from a given conditional probability) and state that P(E|F) is not defined when P(F) = 0
Apply the definition when the elementary events are not equally likely, using a tree diagram to assign probabilities (coin then coin-or-die experiment)
State and use the properties P(S|F) = P(F|F) = 1, P((A or B)|F) = P(A|F) + P(B|F) - P((A and B)|F) (and its disjoint case), and P(E'|F) = 1 - P(E|F)
State the multiplication rule P(E and F) = P(E) P(F|E) = P(F) P(E|F) and use it for successive draws without replacement (urns, cards, oranges)
Extend the multiplication rule to three events, P(E and F and G) = P(E) P(F|E) P(G|EF), and use it for three successive draws
Define independent events by P(E|F) = P(E), P(F|E) = P(F) and equivalently P(E and F) = P(E) P(F); define dependent events; test given events for independence

Distinguish independent events from mutually exclusive events (events with non-zero probabilities cannot be both); state the condition for independent experiments and for three mutually independent events

Prove and use: if E and F are independent then so are E and F', E' and F, E' and F'; P(at least one of A, B) = 1 - P(A') P(B') for independent A, B; find P(neither), P(exactly one), P(A and not B) and probabilities for draws with replacement and repeated throws
Find winning probabilities in a game of alternate independent throws by summing an infinite G.P. (Miscellaneous Example 23)

Define a partition of a sample space (pairwise disjoint, exhaustive, non-zero probabilities), recognise examples such as {E, E'} and {E and F', E and F, E' and F, E' and F'}, and know a partition is not unique
State, prove and apply the theorem of total probability P(A) = sum of P(Ej) P(A|Ej) over a partition
State and prove Bayes' theorem and use its terminology: hypotheses, priori probability P(Ei), a posteriori probability P(Ei|A), formula for the probability of causes
Apply Bayes' theorem to bags and boxes, machines and defective items, medical tests, truth-telling reports, transport and multiple-choice guessing problems with two, three or four hypotheses

concepts.name: Conditional probability from a reduced sample space
concepts.description: Meaning and notation of P(E|F), and finding it for experiments with equally likely outcomes by treating F as the new sample space: P(E|F) = n(E and F)/n(F).
concepts.idea: Knowing that F has occurred removes every outcome outside F, so the probability of E is measured inside F only.
concepts.rule: For equally likely outcomes, P(E|F) = (number of outcomes favourable to both E and F) / (number of outcomes favourable to F).
concepts.example: Three coins: E = at least two heads, F = first coin tail. F = {THH, THT, TTH, TTT}, only THH is in E, so P(E|F) = 1/4.

An instructor has a question bank of 300 easy True/False questions, 200 difficult True/False questions, 500 easy multiple choice questions and 400 difficult multiple choice questions. A question is selected at random. Find the probability that it is an easy question given that it is a multiple choice question.
questions.a: Let E: the question is easy, F: the question is multiple choice. n(F) = 500 + 400 = 900 and n(E and F) = 500. So P(E|F) = n(E and F)/n(F) = 500/900 = 5/9.
s: Identifies the reduced sample space: n(F) = 900 multiple choice questions, of which n(E and F) = 500 are easy

questions.a: Only I

questions.q: Assume each child born is equally likely to be a boy or a girl. A family has two children. Find the conditional probability that both are girls given that (i) the youngest is a girl, (ii) at least one is a girl. Explain why the two answers differ.
questions.a: S = {(b,b), (b,g), (g,b), (g,g)} with elder child written first. (i) F = youngest is a girl = {(b,g), (g,g)}, so P = 1/2. (ii) F = at least one girl = {(b,g), (g,b), (g,g)}, so P = 1/3. The answers differ because the two conditions give different reduced sample spaces: 2 outcomes in (i) but 3 outcomes in (ii), while only (g,g) is favourable in each.
s: (i) Reduced sample space {(b,g), (g,g)}, probability 1/2
(ii) Reduced sample space {(b,g), (g,b), (g,g)}, probability 1/3
Explains that the given event changes the reduced sample space (2 outcomes against 3)

questions.q: A coin is tossed three times. E is 'at least two heads' and F is 'at most two heads'. A student writes P(E|F) = 3/8 because three outcomes have exactly two heads. Is the student right? Justify.
questions.a: No. E and F = {HHT, HTH, THH}, so 3/8 is P(E and F), not P(E|F). Given F, the sample space reduces to F, which has 7 outcomes (all except HHH). So P(E|F) = 3/7.
s: States that 3/8 is P(E and F), because the student divided by n(S) = 8 instead of n(F)

questions.q: For the experiment of rolling one fair die, construct two events E and F such that P(E|F) = 2/3, and verify your answer by listing the outcomes.
questions.a: One example: F = {1, 2, 3} and E = 'the number is odd' = {1, 3, 5}. Then E and F = {1, 3}, n(F) = 3, so P(E|F) = n(E and F)/n(F) = 2/3. (Any F with 3 outcomes of which exactly 2 lie in E, or F with 6 outcomes and 4 in E, is acceptable.)
s: Chooses an event F and lists its outcomes
Chooses E so that exactly two-thirds of the outcomes of F lie in E, listing E and F
Verifies P(E|F) = n(E and F)/n(F) = 2/3

concepts.name: Definition and properties of conditional probability
concepts.description: The definition P(E|F) = P(E and F)/P(F) with P(F) not 0, used with given probabilities and with outcomes that are not equally likely, and the three properties of conditional probability.
concepts.idea: Conditional probability is the share of F's probability that also belongs to E; it behaves like an ordinary probability with F playing the role of the sample space.
concepts.rule: P(E|F) = P(E and F)/P(F), P(F) not 0. P(S|F) = P(F|F) = 1; P((A or B)|F) = P(A|F) + P(B|F) - P((A and B)|F); P(E'|F) = 1 - P(E|F).

questions.q: If E and F are two events of the same sample space and P(F) is not 0, the conditional probability P(E|F) is defined as
questions.a: P(E and F)/P(F)

A coin is tossed. If it shows head, it is tossed again; if it shows tail, a die is thrown. Find the conditional probability of the event 'the die shows a number greater than 4' given that 'there is at least one tail'.
questions.a: The outcomes (H,H), (H,T) have probability 1/4 each and (T,1), ..., (T,6) have probability 1/12 each (not equally likely). F = at least one tail = {(H,T), (T,1), ..., (T,6)}, so P(F) = 1/4 + 6/12 = 3/4. E and F = {(T,5), (T,6)}, so P(E and F) = 2/12 = 1/6. P(E|F) = (1/6)/(3/4) = 2/9.
s: Assigns the unequal probabilities (1/4 and 1/12) and finds P(F) = 3/4

questions.q: An electronic assembly consists of two subsystems A and B. It is known that P(A fails) = 0.25, P(B fails alone) = 0.10 and P(A and B fail) = 0.15. Evaluate (i) P(B fails) (ii) P(A fails | B has failed) (iii) P(A fails alone).
questions.a: (i) P(B fails) = P(B fails alone) + P(A and B fail) = 0.10 + 0.15 = 0.25. (ii) P(A fails | B has failed) = P(A and B fail)/P(B fails) = 0.15/0.25 = 3/5 = 0.6. (iii) P(A fails alone) = P(A fails) - P(A and B fail) = 0.25 - 0.15 = 0.10.
s: P(A fails | B has failed) = 0.15/0.25 = 0.6
P(A fails alone) = 0.25 - 0.15 = 0.10

questions.q: Let A, B and F be events of a sample space S with P(F) not 0. Consider these statements. (I) If A and B are disjoint, then P((A or B)|F) = P(A|F) + P(B|F). (II) P(S|F) = P(F|F) = 1. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Both I and II

questions.q: A and B are two events. (i) Find P(B|A) if A is a subset of B and P(A) is not 0. (ii) Find P(B|A) if A and B have no common outcome and P(A) is not 0. (iii) Show that if A is a subset of B and P(B) is not 0, then P(A|B) is greater than or equal to P(A).
questions.a: (i) If A is a subset of B then A and B = A, so P(B|A) = P(A)/P(A) = 1. (ii) If A and B have no common outcome then P(A and B) = 0, so P(B|A) = 0/P(A) = 0. (iii) P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B) = P(A)/P(B). Since P(B) is at most 1, P(A)/P(B) is at least P(A), so P(A|B) >= P(A).
s: (i) Uses A and B = A to get P(B|A) = 1
(ii) Uses P(A and B) = 0 to get P(B|A) = 0
(iii) P(A|B) = P(A)/P(B) >= P(A) because P(B) <= 1

questions.q: A student claims that P(E|F) + P(E|F') = 1 for all events E and F. Test the claim for a fair die with E = {2} and F = {2, 4, 6}, and state the correct property.
questions.a: P(E|F) = 1/3 and P(E|F') = 0 because 2 is not in F' = {1, 3, 5}. The sum is 1/3, not 1, so the claim is wrong. The correct property keeps the same given event: P(E|F) + P(E'|F) = 1, i.e. P(E'|F) = 1 - P(E|F).
s: Computes P(E|F) = 1/3 and P(E|F') = 0, so the sum is 1/3 and the claim fails
States the correct property P(E'|F) = 1 - P(E|F)

questions.q: Construct values of P(A), P(B) and P(A and B) for two events A and B so that P(A|B) = 1/2 and P(B|A) = 1/4. Verify both conditional probabilities and check that P(A or B) does not exceed 1.
questions.a: One example: P(A and B) = 1/8, P(B) = 1/4, P(A) = 1/2. Then P(A|B) = (1/8)/(1/4) = 1/2 and P(B|A) = (1/8)/(1/2) = 1/4. Also P(A or B) = 1/2 + 1/4 - 1/8 = 5/8, which is not more than 1, so the values are consistent. (Any values with P(B) = 2 P(A and B), P(A) = 4 P(A and B) and P(A or B) <= 1 are acceptable.)
s: Chooses values with P(B) = 2 P(A and B) and P(A) = 4 P(A and B)
Verifies P(A|B) = 1/2 and P(B|A) = 1/4 by the definition
Checks P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B) is at most 1

concepts.name: Multiplication theorem on probability
concepts.description: Finding the probability of the simultaneous occurrence of two or three events as P(E) P(F|E) and P(E) P(F|E) P(G|EF), especially for draws without replacement.
concepts.idea: The chance that E and F both happen is the chance of E times the chance of F once E is known to have happened.
concepts.rule: P(E and F) = P(E) P(F|E) = P(F) P(E|F); P(E and F and G) = P(E) P(F|E) P(G|EF).
concepts.example: Urn with 10 black and 5 white balls, two drawn without replacement: P(both black) = (10/15)(9/14) = 3/7.

A bag contains 4 red and 3 blue balls. Two balls are drawn one after the other without replacement. Using the multiplication rule, find the probability that the first ball is red and the second ball is blue.
questions.a: Let E: first ball red, F: second ball blue. P(E) = 4/7. After a red ball is removed, 6 balls remain of which 3 are blue, so P(F|E) = 3/6 = 1/2. P(E and F) = P(E) P(F|E) = (4/7)(1/2) = 2/7.

questions.q: A bag contains 5 white, 4 red and 3 black balls. Three balls are drawn one after another without replacement. Find the probability that the first is white, the second is red and the third is black.
questions.a: Let W, R, B be the events first white, second red, third black. P(W) = 5/12. P(R|W) = 4/11, since 11 balls remain and 4 are red. P(B|WR) = 3/10, since 10 balls remain and 3 are black. P(W and R and B) = P(W) P(R|W) P(B|WR) = (5/12)(4/11)(3/10) = 60/1320 = 1/22.
s: P(B|WR) = 3/10 with the total reduced to 10

questions.q: An urn contains 10 black and 5 white balls. Two balls are drawn one after the other. Find (i) P(both black) when drawn without replacement, (ii) P(first black and second white) when drawn without replacement, (iii) P(both black) when the first ball is replaced before the second draw, and say why (i) and (iii) differ.
questions.a: (i) (10/15)(9/14) = 3/7. (ii) (10/15)(5/14) = 5/21. (iii) With replacement the urn is unchanged, so (10/15)(10/15) = 4/9. They differ because without replacement the conditional probability P(F|E) = 9/14 is smaller than P(F) = 10/15: removing a black ball changes the urn for the second draw.
s: (iii) 4/9, and explains that without replacement P(F|E) = 9/14 differs from 10/15

questions.q: Ravi finds the probability of drawing two kings, one after the other without replacement from a pack of 52 cards, as (4/52) x (4/52) = 1/169. Evaluate his working.
questions.a: He is wrong. After one king is drawn and not replaced, 51 cards remain with 3 kings, so P(second king | first king) = 3/51, not 4/52. By the multiplication rule the probability is (4/52)(3/51) = 1/221.
s: Identifies the error: the second factor must be the conditional probability 3/51
Correct answer (4/52)(3/51) = 1/221

questions.q: Create a problem about drawing three balls without replacement from an urn of your own choice which needs the multiplication rule for three events, and solve it.
questions.a: Example: An urn has 4 red and 3 green balls. Three balls are drawn one after another without replacement. Find the probability that all three are red. Solution: P(R1) = 4/7, P(R2|R1) = 3/6, P(R3|R1R2) = 2/5. So P(R1 and R2 and R3) = (4/7)(3/6)(2/5) = 24/210 = 4/35.
s: States a clear three-draw, without-replacement problem with the urn contents given
Writes the three factors P(E), P(F|E), P(G|EF) with numerators and denominators reduced correctly
Multiplies to a correct final probability

concepts.name: Independent events: definition and test
concepts.description: Independence of two events as P(E|F) = P(E), equivalently P(E and F) = P(E) P(F); dependent events; testing a given pair of events for independence.
concepts.idea: Two events are independent when the occurrence of one does not change the probability of the other.
concepts.rule: E and F are independent if and only if P(E and F) = P(E) P(F); otherwise they are dependent.
concepts.example: Die: E = multiple of 3 = {3, 6}, F = even = {2, 4, 6}. P(E and F) = 1/6 = (1/3)(1/2), so E and F are independent.

concepts.idea: Independence carries over to complements, which turns 'at least one', 'neither' and 'exactly one' problems into products; it is a different idea from mutual exclusiveness.
concepts.rule: If E and F are independent, so are E and F', E' and F, E' and F'. P(at least one of A, B) = 1 - P(A') P(B'). Mutually exclusive events with non-zero probabilities are never independent.
concepts.example: A and B solve a problem independently with probabilities 1/2 and 1/3: P(solved) = 1 - (1/2)(2/3) = 2/3.

concepts.name: Partition of a sample space and the theorem of total probability
concepts.description: Recognising a partition (pairwise disjoint, exhaustive, non-zero probabilities) and finding P(A) as the sum of P(Ej) P(A|Ej) over the partition.
concepts.idea: An event that can happen through several mutually exclusive routes has probability equal to the sum of (probability of the route) x (probability of the event along that route).
concepts.rule: If {E1, ..., En} is a partition of S with each P(Ej) not 0, then P(A) = P(E1) P(A|E1) + ... + P(En) P(A|En).
concepts.example: P(strike) = 0.65, P(on time | strike) = 0.32, P(on time | no strike) = 0.80: P(on time) = 0.65 x 0.32 + 0.35 x 0.80 = 0.488.

concepts.name: Bayes' theorem
concepts.description: Finding the reverse (a posteriori) probability P(Ei|A) of a hypothesis from the priori probabilities P(Ei) and the conditional probabilities P(A|Ei), with the terminology of hypotheses and causes.
concepts.idea: Once the outcome A is seen, each cause Ei gets the fraction of P(A) that came through it.

concepts.example: Bag I: 3 red, 4 black; Bag II: 5 red, 6 black; a red ball is drawn from a bag chosen at random. P(Bag II | red) = (1/2)(5/11) / [(1/2)(3/7) + (1/2)(5/11)] = 35/68.

questions.q: A laboratory blood test is 99% effective in detecting a certain disease when it is in fact present. However, the test also yields a false positive result for 0.5% of the healthy persons tested. If 0.1 percent of the population actually has the disease, find the probability that a person has the disease given that his test result is positive, and explain why it is far smaller than 0.99.
questions.a: Let E: person has the disease, A: test is positive. P(E) = 0.001, P(E') = 0.999, P(A|E) = 0.99, P(A|E') = 0.005. By Bayes' theorem, P(E|A) = (0.001)(0.99) / [(0.001)(0.99) + (0.999)(0.005)] = 0.00099/(0.00099 + 0.004995) = 0.00099/0.005985 = 22/133, about 0.165. It is far below 0.99 because the disease is very rare: the healthy group is so large that its false positives (0.004995) outnumber the true positives (0.00099).
s: Applies Bayes' theorem to get 0.00099/0.005985 = 22/133 (about 0.165)
Explains that the tiny prior makes false positives from the large healthy group dominate the denominator

questions.q: If a machine is correctly set up it produces 90% acceptable items; if incorrectly set up, only 40%. 80% of the set ups are correctly done. After a certain set up the machine produces 2 acceptable items. A student gives the probability that the machine is correctly set up as 0.8 x 0.9 x 0.9 = 0.648. Evaluate this answer.
questions.a: The answer is wrong: 0.648 is only the numerator P(B1) P(A|B1) of Bayes' formula, i.e. P(B1 and A). It must be divided by P(A) = 0.8 x 0.9 x 0.9 + 0.2 x 0.4 x 0.4 = 0.648 + 0.032 = 0.680. So P(B1|A) = 0.648/0.680 = 81/85, about 0.95.
s: Identifies that 0.648 is only the numerator and the total-probability denominator 0.680 is missing

questions.q: Create a problem about two machines producing items, some of which are defective, in which the probability that a defective item came from the first machine works out to exactly 3/4. Solve it using Bayes' theorem.
questions.a: Example: Machines A and B each produce 50% of the items; 3% of A's items and 1% of B's items are defective. An item chosen at random is defective; find the probability that it came from A. Solution: P(A) = P(B) = 0.5, P(D|A) = 0.03, P(D|B) = 0.01. P(A|D) = (0.5)(0.03) / [(0.5)(0.03) + (0.5)(0.01)] = 0.015/0.020 = 3/4.
s: States a complete problem giving each machine's share of output and its defective rate
Writes Bayes' formula with the total-probability denominator for the chosen numbers
Evaluates the posterior probability to exactly 3/4
